Zimri
ZIM-rye
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Zimri (H2174); uncertain meaning, possibly "my song" or "my praise" (from zamar, "to sing, make music"). The same name was borne by the Simeonite man speared by Phinehas at Peor (Num 25:14).

📖 Biblical Definition

Zimri (c. 885 BC, seven-day reign) was the fifth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:9-20), captain of half the chariots under Elah son of Baasha, whose coup against his master produced one of the shortest reigns in the entire Bible and one of its most dramatic ends. After assassinating Elah at Tirzah and killing every male of Baasha's house, Zimri took the throne; but when the army at Gibbethon heard the news they immediately proclaimed their general Omri king and marched on Tirzah. Within seven days Omri's forces had besieged the city; Zimri, seeing capture inevitable, went into the inner room of the king's palace and burned the palace down around himself rather than be taken (1 Kings 16:18). His name became a byword in Israel: when Jehu's revolt was approaching some seventy years later, Jezebel called to him from her window: "Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?" (2 Kings 9:31) — a sneering reference to the brief and disastrous fate of the previous master-killing coup-leader. His seven-day reign embodies one strand of the divided-monarchy pattern: usurpation without prophetic mandate ends quickly and badly.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Fifth king of Israel (c. 885 BC); chariot-commander under Elah; reigned only 7 days; burned the palace down around himself rather than be captured by Omri's army; became a byword for treacherous usurpation (Jezebel taunted Jehu: 'Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?').

ZIMRI, proper noun. Hebrew Zimri (H2174); uncertain meaning, possibly "my song."

Fifth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 885 BC); originally chariot-commander under Elah.

Reigned only 7 days; assassinated Elah, killed all of Baasha's house, then was besieged by Omri's army at Tirzah and burned the palace down around himself.

Distinct from Zimri the Simeonite speared by Phinehas at Peor (Num 25:14), and from Zimri son of Zerah (1 Chr 2:6).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Kings 16:15-18 — "In the twenty and seventh year of Asa king of Judah did Zimri reign seven days in Tirzah... And it came to pass, when Zimri saw that the city was taken, that he went into the palace of the king's house, and burnt the king's house over him with fire, and died."

1 Kings 16:19 — "For his sins which he sinned in doing evil in the sight of the LORD, in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin which he did, to make Israel to sin."

2 Kings 9:31 — "And as Jehu entered in at the gate, [Jezebel] said, Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?"

Proverbs 21:25-26 — "The desire of the slothful killeth him; for his hands refuse to labour. He coveteth greedily all the day long..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Zimri is corrupted when his seven-day reign is treated as theatrical irrelevance rather than as the canonical example of usurpation-without-prophetic-mandate, or when Jezebel's later taunt is read as merely insulting Jehu without recognizing the doctrinal point her insult was making.

expand to see more

Seven-day-reign as theater. The dramatic detail of Zimri's suicide-by-arson is sometimes treated as the most memorable thing about him — a colorful Tirzah-palace scene rather than a doctrinal datum. The narrator's interest is theological: even after fulfilling the prior prophecy (the extermination of Baasha's house), Zimri's reign was illegitimate because no prophet had been sent to anoint him as king. He was the instrument of one judgment but possessed no mandate for his own dynasty. The seven-day collapse demonstrates the principle: God's instruments of judgment are not automatically God's chosen rulers.

Jezebel's taunt over-personalized. When Jehu came in his coup against the house of Ahab (2 Kings 9), Jezebel called from her window: 'Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?' (2 Kings 9:31). The taunt is often read as Jezebel's defiant personal insult — calling Jehu another fly-by-night usurper like Zimri seventy years earlier. The fuller doctrinal weight is that Jezebel may have been technically right about the parallel and entirely wrong about its meaning: Jehu, unlike Zimri, had been anointed by a prophet sent from Elisha (2 Kings 9:1-10). The same kind of coup with prophetic mandate became the longest northern dynasty (Jehu — Jehoahaz — Joash — Jeroboam II — Zachariah; ninety-plus years).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Zimri (H2174); uncertain meaning, possibly "my song." Fifth king of Israel (c. 885 BC); 7-day reign; suicide by palace arson.
